extracted.intended_audience: community college administrators, faculty, and staff preparing grant/project proposals
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for preparing competitive community-college project proposals for external funding, emphasizing compliance with funder criteria, specificity, fiscal soundness, and documented community involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meet the criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sure that the proposal meets the criteria of the funding agency; careful reading of the restrictions and guidelines is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The document repeatedly warns that not meeting funder criteria is a fatal flaw. Example: proposals that requested funding for on-campus student/faculty projects when the grant was for off-campus community programs would be ineligible. Follow the directions exactly; if a proposal does not meet stated objectives, it may be rejected even if funds are otherwise available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present Specific Facts and Plans
rubrics_metrics.description: List specific classes, forums and seminars identified as to topic, cost and duration rather than proposing indeterminate activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators prefer proposals that enumerate concrete activities with topics, costs, and durations. For community-targeted projects, identify disadvantaged areas by citing designations from private or governmental agencies; substantiate claimed community need with supporting material (e.g., newspaper reprints). Avoid vague statements like 'topics to be determined' or undetermined costs/lengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantiate community need with external evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide evidence beyond the proposing institution to verify that the stated need exists in the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include reprints of relevant newspaper articles, citations, or formal designations from agencies indicating high unemployment, low income, or economic distress. Proposals making unverified or indefinite claims of need are less likely to be funded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make proposal development a year-round effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain continuous communication with community contacts and college personnel about needs; keep a proposal bank to reflect ongoing community needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals that arise from sustained community engagement (e.g., minutes of meetings held months earlier) are stronger than last-minute ideas. Example: an idea from a proposal file led to a successful Mobile Advisement Center. Continual communication shows the project responds to genuine need rather than being a spur-of-the-moment submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propose economic solutions to problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Design cost-effective interventions; avoid high unit costs per participant when cheaper local options exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't plan small-group seminars with prohibitive per-participant costs if the same training could be offered through regular classes at local institutions. Be cautious about using high-paid consultants—evaluators react negatively to excessive consultant use and to unnecessary travel/flying in of experts when qualified local personnel exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document the involvement of persons and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Include supporting material (letters, resolutions) that documents commitment from partnering institutions and the involvement of key personnel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For consortia, include letters from college presidents or copies of board resolutions confirming support, funding, and involvement. If the project's success depends on key people, include short resumes. While 'projects, not people, are supposed to be funded,' panels may be influenced by outstanding qualifications or past successful implementations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triple check your figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure budget accuracy and internal consistency; check for arithmetic errors and unrealistic salary projections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of errors: a part-time position projected to yield an annual income of over $50,000 if projected to full time; budgets that do not balance. Have financial figures reviewed by the bursar or business manager to verify accuracy and realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check out the proposal on campus before submitting
rubrics_metrics.description: Have multiple, disinterested reviewers edit and critique the proposal prior to submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit the proposal to several persons for editing and reactions: ask an English or journalism instructor to check spelling and language quality; have a bursar/business manager review the budget; take it to disinterested readers (not subordinates) and ask whether they would fund it. In the absence of a development office, this internal vetting substitutes for formal review infrastructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid superficial, irrelevant, or last-minute proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not submit proposals that appear amateurish, irrelevant to the community problem, or hastily assembled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The evaluator criticizes proposals that 'had no soul,' were 'in-house solutions to an out-house problem,' or touted supposed 'new, innovative programs' that were not novel. Proposals that are last-minute, wild, or poorly justified weaken competitiveness in a crowded, competitive selection process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for competitive selection: specific, documented, fiscally sound
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that panels select among competing submissions; proposals should meet funder criteria, be specific, economical, well-documented, and fiscally sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This summary criterion consolidates the article's central evaluative lens: competitive funding means panels favor proposals that demonstrate clarity of purpose, documented community need/support, realistic budgets, cost-effectiveness, and responsiveness to agency guidelines. Self-evaluate proposals against these dimensions before submission.
